reminder: A map is continuous when the preimage of every [open set](c:open-set) is open.
definition: A map $f:X\to Y$ between [topological spaces](c:topological-space) is continuous when $f^{-1}(U)$ is an [open set](c:open-set) of $X$ for every open set $U$ of $Y$. For [metric spaces](c:metric-space) this means: for every $x$ and every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ such that $d(x,x')<\delta$ implies $d(f(x),f(x'))<\varepsilon$.
examples: The identity map and every constant map are continuous.
Polynomials $\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ are continuous, and so are $\sin$ and $\exp$.
Non-example: the step function with $f(x)=0$ for $x<0$ and $f(x)=1$ for $x\ge0$ is not continuous, because $f^{-1}((1/2,2))=[0,\infty)$ is not open.

steps: Give each topological space its Borel [sigma-algebra](c:sigma-algebra), the smallest one that contains all open sets.
For a continuous map $f$, the preimage of each open set is open, so it is measurable.
The sets with a measurable preimage form a sigma-algebra, so they include all Borel sets.
Hence $f$ is a measurable function between the two Borel measurable spaces.
links.why: It shows that every result about measurable functions also holds for continuous functions.

steps: Start with a continuous function $f:X\to Y$.
Add the condition that $f$ is a bijection.
Add the condition that the inverse $f^{-1}$ is also continuous.
Then $f$ is a [homeomorphism](c:homeomorphism).
links.why: It shows what a homeomorphism adds to continuity: a continuous inverse.

steps: Let $f$ be a [smooth function](c:smooth-function), so it has derivatives of every order.
A function with a derivative at a point is continuous at that point.
So every smooth function is continuous.
The smooth case adds that the derivatives of all orders exist.
links.why: It shows that smoothness is continuity plus derivatives of all orders.

reminder: A holomorphic function has a complex [derivative](c:derivative) at every point of its open domain.
definition: A function $f:U\to\mathbb{C}$ on an [open set](c:open-set) $U\subseteq\mathbb{C}$ is holomorphic when the limit $f'(z)=\lim_{h\to0}(f(z+h)-f(z))/h$ exists for every $z\in U$, where $h$ is a [complex number](c:complex-number). This limit is the [derivative](c:derivative) of $f$, and it must be the same for every way that $h$ tends to $0$.
examples: Polynomials in $z$, $e^z$, $\sin z$ and $\cos z$ are holomorphic on all of $\mathbb{C}$.
The function $1/z$ is holomorphic on $\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0\}$.
Non-example: $f(z)=\bar z$ is not holomorphic, because the difference quotient is $1$ along the real axis and $-1$ along the imaginary axis.

steps: Identify $\mathbb{C}$ with the plane $\mathbb{R}^2$ and write $f=u+iv$.
A complex derivative gives the approximation $f(z+h)\approx f(z)+f'(z)h$, which is real-linear in $h$.
So $f$ is differentiable as a map from $\mathbb{R}^2$ to $\mathbb{R}^2$.
The holomorphic case adds that this linear map is multiplication by a complex number, which gives the Cauchy-Riemann equations.
links.why: It shows that complex differentiability is real differentiability plus one linearity condition.

steps: Start with a holomorphic function $f$ on an open set $U$.
Choose $U=\mathbb{C}$, the whole plane.
A holomorphic function on all of $\mathbb{C}$ is an [entire function](c:entire-function).
links.why: It shows that an entire function is a holomorphic function with the largest possible domain.

steps: Take a holomorphic function $f:U\to V$ between open sets.
Add the condition that $f$ is a bijection onto $V$.
A bijective holomorphic map has a holomorphic inverse, so $f$ is a [biholomorphic function](c:biholomorphic-function).
links.why: It shows that a biholomorphic map is a holomorphic bijection, with no extra check on the inverse.

reminder: Every [open cover](c:open-cover) of a compact space has a finite subcover.
definition: A [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ is compact when, for every family of [open sets](c:open-set) with union $X$, finitely many of them already have union $X$. Equivalently, every [open cover](c:open-cover) of $X$ has a finite subcover.
examples: The closed interval $[0,1]$ is compact, and so is every closed bounded subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ (Heine-Borel).
Every finite topological space is compact.
Non-example: $\mathbb{R}$ is not compact, because the open cover $\{(-n,n):n\in\mathbb{N}\}$ has no finite subcover.
Non-example: $(0,1)$ is not compact, because the open cover $\{(1/n,1):n\ge2\}$ has no finite subcover.

steps: Start with a compact space $X$.
Add the condition that any two distinct points of $X$ have disjoint open neighbourhoods.
Then $X$ is a [compact Hausdorff space](c:compact-hausdorff-space).
links.why: It shows that compact Hausdorff spaces keep every property of compact spaces and add the separation of points.

steps: Let $X$ be compact and let $\mathcal U$ be an open cover of $X$.
By compactness, a finite subfamily of $\mathcal U$ still covers $X$.
A finite subfamily is countable.
So every open cover has a countable subcover, and $X$ is a [Lindelöf space](c:lindelof-space).
links.why: It shows that compactness is the strong form of the Lindelöf property, with finite in place of countable.

reminder: A Hilbert space is an [inner product space](c:inner-product-space) that is complete for its induced norm.
definition: A Hilbert space is a real or complex [inner product space](c:inner-product-space) $H$ in which every [Cauchy sequence](c:cauchy-sequence) for the norm $\|x\|=\sqrt{\langle x,x\rangle}$ converges to a point of $H$. Equivalently, $H$ is a [complete metric space](c:complete-metric-space) for the metric $\|x-y\|$.
examples: $\mathbb{R}^n$ and $\mathbb{C}^n$ with the usual inner product are Hilbert spaces.
The space $\ell^2$ of square-summable sequences and the space $L^2(\mu)$ for a measure $\mu$ are Hilbert spaces.

Non-example: the continuous functions on $[0,1]$ with $\langle f,g\rangle=\int_0^1 f\bar g$ form an inner product space that is not complete, because continuous functions can approach a step function.

steps: Take the norm $\|x\|=\sqrt{\langle x,x\rangle}$ that comes from the inner product.
This is a norm, so $H$ is a normed space.
Completeness for this norm is exactly the Banach condition.
So every Hilbert space is a [Banach space](c:banach-space).
links.why: It shows that every theorem about Banach spaces applies to Hilbert spaces, which add an inner product.

steps: Start with an inner product space $V$ and its induced norm.
Add the condition that every Cauchy sequence in $V$ converges in $V$.
Then $V$ is a Hilbert space.
links.why: It names the one extra condition, completeness, that separates Hilbert spaces from inner product spaces.

reminder: A function is integrable when it is measurable and its absolute value has a finite integral.
definition: A [measurable function](c:measurable-function) $f$ on a [measure](c:measure) space $(X,\mu)$ is integrable when $\int_X|f|\,d\mu<\infty$, where the integral is the [Lebesgue integral](c:lebesgue-integral). Then $\int_X f\,d\mu$ is a well-defined number.
examples: A bounded measurable function on a set of finite measure is integrable, for example $\sin x$ on $[0,2\pi]$.
The function $e^{-|x|}$ is integrable on $\mathbb{R}$, with integral $2$.
Non-example: $f(x)=1/x$ on $(0,1]$ is measurable but not integrable, because $\int_0^1 dx/x=\infty$.
Non-example: $\sin x/x$ on $\mathbb{R}$ is not Lebesgue integrable, because $\int|\sin x/x|\,dx=\infty$.

steps: Start with an integrable function $f$.
By definition, $f$ is measurable.
Integrability adds one condition: the integral of $|f|$ is finite.
links.why: It shows that integrability is measurability plus a bound on the size of $f$.

reminder: A prime number is a natural number greater than 1 whose only positive divisors are 1 and itself.
definition: A prime number is a [natural number](c:natural-number) $p>1$ such that the only positive [divisors](c:divisibility) of $p$ are $1$ and $p$. Equivalently, $p>1$ and $p\mid ab$ implies $p\mid a$ or $p\mid b$ (Euclid's lemma).
examples: The first primes are $2,3,5,7,11,13$.
The number $2$ is the only even prime.
Non-example: $1$ is not prime, because the definition needs $p>1$.
Non-example: $9=3\cdot3$ is not prime, because $3$ is a divisor other than $1$ and $9$.

steps: Work in the ring $\mathbb{Z}$ of integers.
Let $p$ be a prime number.
By Euclid's lemma, $p\mid ab$ implies $p\mid a$ or $p\mid b$.
So $p$ is a [prime element](c:prime-element) of $\mathbb{Z}$.
links.why: It shows that prime numbers are the positive prime elements of $\mathbb{Z}$, the model case for prime elements of any ring.

reminder: A Banach space is a [normed space](c:normed-space) in which every Cauchy sequence converges.
definition: A Banach space is a [normed space](c:normed-space) $(X,\|\cdot\|)$ over $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$ that is complete: every [Cauchy sequence](c:cauchy-sequence) for the metric $\|x-y\|$ converges to an element of $X$. Equivalently, it is a [complete metric space](c:complete-metric-space) whose metric comes from a norm.
examples: $\mathbb{R}^n$ with any norm is a Banach space.
The space $C([0,1])$ with the sup norm, and the spaces $\ell^p$ and $L^p$ for $1\le p\le\infty$, are Banach spaces.
Non-example: $C([0,1])$ with the norm $\|f\|_1=\int_0^1|f|$ is a normed space that is not complete.

steps: Start with a Banach space $X$.
By definition, $X$ is a normed space.
The extra condition is that every Cauchy sequence converges in $X$.
links.why: It shows that completeness is the only thing a Banach space adds to a normed space.

steps: Give $X$ the metric $d(x,y)=\|x-y\|$.
This is a metric, so $X$ is a metric space.
Completeness for this metric is the Banach condition.
So $X$ is a [complete metric space](c:complete-metric-space).
links.why: It shows that results about complete metric spaces, such as the Baire theorem, apply to Banach spaces.

steps: Take a Banach space $X$ whose norm satisfies the parallelogram law.
Define $\langle x,y\rangle$ from the norm by the polarization identity.
This is an inner product with $\langle x,x\rangle=\|x\|^2$.
So $X$ is a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space).
links.why: It shows when a Banach space is a Hilbert space: when its norm comes from an inner product.

reminder: A set is convex when it contains the whole [line segment](c:line-segment) between any two of its points.
definition: A [subset](c:subset) $C$ of a real [vector space](c:vector-space) is convex when $tx+(1-t)y\in C$ for all $x,y\in C$ and all $t\in[0,1]$. In words, $C$ contains the [line segment](c:line-segment) between any two of its points.
examples: Balls, half-spaces and affine subspaces of $\mathbb{R}^n$ are convex.
The convex subsets of $\mathbb{R}$ are exactly the intervals.
Non-example: a circle in the plane is not convex, because the midpoint of two opposite points lies off the circle.
Non-example: $[0,1]\cup[2,3]$ is not convex, because the point $1.5$ lies between $1$ and $2$ but not in the set.

steps: Take a convex set $C$ in a real vector space.
Add the condition that $\lambda x\in C$ for all $x\in C$ and all $\lambda>0$.
Then $C$ is a [convex cone](c:convex-cone).
links.why: It shows that a convex cone is a convex set with one more closure condition.

steps: Take a convex set $C$ in a real topological vector space.
Add the condition that $C$ is compact.
Then $C$ is a [compact convex set](c:compact-convex-set).
links.why: It shows that a compact convex set is a convex set with compactness added.

reminder: A [set](c:set) is finite when it has exactly $n$ elements for some natural number $n$.
definition: A [set](c:set) $A$ is finite when there is a [bijection](c:bijection) from $A$ onto $\{1,\dots,n\}$ for some [natural number](c:natural-number) $n\ge0$. The number $n$ is the size of $A$, and $n=0$ gives the empty set.
examples: The empty set and $\{a,b,c\}$ are finite sets.
The set of divisors of $12$ is finite, with size $6$.
Non-example: $\mathbb{N}$ is not finite, because the first $n+1$ natural numbers cannot map injectively into $\{1,\dots,n\}$.
Non-example: the interval $[0,1]$ is not finite, because it contains the infinite set $\{1/k:k\ge1\}$.

steps: Let $A$ be finite, with a bijection $g:A\to\{1,\dots,n\}$.
Since $\{1,\dots,n\}\subseteq\mathbb{N}$, the map $g$ is an injection of $A$ into $\mathbb{N}$.
A set with an injection into $\mathbb{N}$ is [countable](c:countable-set) in the wide sense.
links.why: It shows that finite sets are the smallest countable sets, and that countable results include the finite case.

reminder: A smooth manifold looks like $\mathbb{R}^n$ near each point, and its charts change by smooth maps.
definition: A smooth manifold is a [manifold](c:manifold) $M$ with an [atlas](c:atlas) of charts $\varphi_i:U_i\to\mathbb{R}^n$ whose transition maps $\varphi_j\circ\varphi_i^{-1}$ are [smooth functions](c:smooth-function). Two such atlases give the same [smooth structure](c:smooth-structure) when their union is again smooth.
examples: The sphere $S^n$ and the torus $S^1\times S^1$ are smooth manifolds.
$\mathbb{R}^n$ is a smooth manifold with one chart, the identity.
Non-example: the union of the two coordinate axes in the plane is not a manifold, because near the origin it is not homeomorphic to an open interval.
Non-example: the closed interval $[0,1]$ is a manifold with boundary, not a manifold, because the endpoints have no neighbourhood homeomorphic to an open interval.

steps: Start with a smooth manifold $M$ and its smooth atlas.
Each chart is a homeomorphism onto an open set of $\mathbb{R}^n$, so $M$ is a topological manifold.
The smooth case adds that all transition maps are smooth.
links.why: It shows that a smooth manifold is a topological manifold with extra structure for calculus.

steps: Take a smooth manifold $M$.
Choose on each tangent space an inner product that varies smoothly with the point.
The result is a [Riemannian manifold](c:riemannian-manifold).
links.why: It shows that a Riemannian manifold is a smooth manifold with a metric added; partitions of unity always give one.

steps: Take a smooth manifold $G$.
Give $G$ a group structure.
Require that multiplication and inversion are smooth maps.
Then $G$ is a [Lie group](c:lie-group).
links.why: It shows that a Lie group is a smooth manifold whose points also multiply smoothly.

reminder: A probability measure is a measure that gives the whole space total mass one.
definition: A probability measure on a [sigma-algebra](c:sigma-algebra) $\mathcal{F}$ of subsets of a set $\Omega$ is a [measure](c:measure) $P:\mathcal{F}\to[0,\infty]$ with $P(\Omega)=1$. So $P$ is countably additive on disjoint sets, and every value lies in $[0,1]$.
examples: Lebesgue measure restricted to $[0,1]$ is a probability measure.
A fair die gives $P(\{k\})=1/6$ for $k=1,\dots,6$ on the power set of $\{1,\dots,6\}$.
The Dirac measure $\delta_x$ at a point $x$ is a probability measure.
Non-example: Lebesgue measure on $\mathbb{R}$ is a measure but not a probability measure, because the whole line has infinite measure.

steps: Start with a probability measure $P$ on $(\Omega,\mathcal{F})$.
It is countably additive and $P(\emptyset)=0$, so it is a [measure](c:measure).
The probability case adds the normalization $P(\Omega)=1$.
links.why: It shows that every result about measures holds for probability measures, which add total mass one.

steps: Fix a point $x\in\Omega$.
Define $\delta_x(A)=1$ when $x\in A$ and $\delta_x(A)=0$ otherwise.
This map is countably additive and $\delta_x(\Omega)=1$.
So $\delta_x$ is a probability measure, the [Dirac measure](c:dirac-measure) at $x$.
links.why: It gives the simplest probability measures, with all mass at one point.

reminder: A polynomial is a finite sum of coefficients times nonnegative powers of a variable.
definition: A polynomial over a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring) $R$ is an expression $a_0+a_1x+\dots+a_nx^n$ with coefficients $a_i\in R$ and $n\ge0$. Two polynomials are equal when all their coefficients are equal; sums and products follow the usual rules for powers of $x$.
examples: $x^2-2$ is a polynomial over $\mathbb{Z}$, and $3$ is a constant polynomial.
$x^3+x$ is a nonzero polynomial over the field with two elements, although it vanishes at every point of that field.
Non-example: $x^{-1}+1$ and $\sqrt{x}$ are not polynomials, because the powers of $x$ must be nonnegative whole numbers.
Non-example: $1+x+x^2+\cdots$ is not a polynomial, because it has infinitely many nonzero terms.

steps: Take a polynomial $a_0+a_1x+\dots+a_nx^n$.
Set $a_k=0$ for every $k>n$.
Then $\sum_{k\ge0}a_kx^k$ is a [power series](c:power-series) with finitely many nonzero terms.
links.why: It shows that a polynomial is a power series that stops, so no convergence question arises.

steps: Take a nonconstant polynomial $f$ over a field $K$.
Require that $f=gh$ forces $g$ or $h$ to be constant.
Then $f$ is an [irreducible polynomial](c:irreducible-polynomial).
links.why: It shows that irreducible polynomials are the polynomials that do not factor, as primes do for integers.

steps: Take a polynomial $a_0+a_1x+\dots+a_nx^n$.
Keep only one term, $a_kx^k$.
The result is a [monomial](c:monomial), a building block of every polynomial.
links.why: It shows that every polynomial is a finite sum of monomials.

reminder: In an algebraically closed field, every nonconstant polynomial has a root.
definition: A [field](c:field) $K$ is algebraically closed when every nonconstant [polynomial](c:polynomial) in $K[x]$ has a [root](c:root-of-a-polynomial) in $K$. Then every such polynomial splits into linear factors over $K$.
examples: The complex numbers $\mathbb{C}$ form an algebraically closed field (the fundamental theorem of algebra).
The field of algebraic numbers, the algebraic closure of $\mathbb{Q}$, is algebraically closed.
Non-example: $\mathbb{R}$ is not algebraically closed, because $x^2+1$ has no real root.
Non-example: no finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$ is algebraically closed, because $1+\prod_{a\in\mathbb{F}_q}(x-a)$ has no root in it.

steps: Start with an algebraically closed field $K$.
By definition, $K$ is a [field](c:field).
The extra condition is that each nonconstant polynomial over $K$ has a root in $K$.
links.why: It shows that algebraic closure is a root condition added to the field axioms.

reminder: A differentiable function has a [derivative](c:derivative) at every point of its domain.
definition: A function $f$ on an open subset $U$ of $\mathbb{R}$ is differentiable when the [limit](c:limit-of-a-function) $f'(x)=\lim_{h\to0}(f(x+h)-f(x))/h$ exists for every $x\in U$, which is the [derivative](c:derivative). In several variables, $f$ is differentiable at $x$ when $f(x+h)=f(x)+Lh+o(|h|)$ for a [linear map](c:linear-map) $L$.
examples: Polynomials, $\sin$ and $\exp$ are differentiable on $\mathbb{R}$.
The function $|x|$ is differentiable at every $x\ne0$.
Non-example: $|x|$ is not differentiable at $0$, because the difference quotient is $1$ for $h>0$ and $-1$ for $h<0$.
Non-example: the Weierstrass function is continuous but differentiable at no point.

steps: Let $f$ be differentiable at $x$, so $f(x+h)-f(x)=f'(x)h+o(h)$.
Let $h\to0$; the right side tends to $0$.
So $f(x+h)\to f(x)$, and $f$ is [continuous](c:continuous-function) at $x$.
Differentiability adds a linear approximation to continuity.
links.why: It shows that differentiability is a stronger form of continuity.

steps: Take a differentiable function $f$.
Require that $f'$ is also differentiable, and so on for every order.
Then $f$ is a [smooth function](c:smooth-function).
links.why: It shows that smoothness repeats differentiability at every order.

reminder: A sequence of functions converges uniformly when the largest error over all points tends to zero.
definition: A sequence of [functions](c:function) $f_n:X\to\mathbb{R}$ converges uniformly to $f$ when for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $N$ with $|f_n(x)-f(x)|<\varepsilon$ for all $n\ge N$ and all $x\in X$. Equivalently, $\sup_x|f_n(x)-f(x)|$ has [limit](c:limit-of-a-sequence) $0$ as $n\to\infty$, so $N$ does not depend on $x$.
examples: $f_n(x)=x/n$ converges uniformly to $0$ on $[0,1]$, because the supremum of the error is $1/n$.
The partial sums of $\sum x^k$ converge uniformly on $[-1/2,1/2]$.
Non-example: $f_n(x)=x^n$ on $[0,1]$ converges pointwise to a discontinuous function, so the convergence is not uniform, because a uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous.
Non-example: $f_n(x)=x/n$ on $\mathbb{R}$ converges pointwise to $0$ but not uniformly, because the supremum of the error is infinite.

steps: Suppose $f_n\to f$ uniformly.
Fix a point $x$; then $|f_n(x)-f(x)|\le\sup_y|f_n(y)-f(y)|\to0$.
So $f_n(x)\to f(x)$ at each $x$, which is [pointwise convergence](c:pointwise-convergence).
Uniform convergence adds that the speed does not depend on $x$.
links.why: It shows that uniform convergence implies pointwise convergence, and what it adds.

reminder: Two events are independent when the probability of both is the product of their probabilities.
definition: Events $A$ and $B$ of a [probability measure](c:probability-measure) $P$ are independent when $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$. [Random variables](c:random-variable) $X$ and $Y$ are independent when $P(X\in S,\,Y\in T)=P(X\in S)P(Y\in T)$ for all [measurable sets](c:measurable-set) $S$ and $T$. A family is independent when this holds for every finite subfamily.
examples: Two tosses of a fair coin: the events first toss heads and second toss heads are independent.
A fair die: $A=\{2,4,6\}$ and $B=\{1,2,3,4\}$ are independent, because $P(A\cap B)=1/3=(1/2)(2/3)$.
Non-example: two disjoint events of positive probability are not independent, because $P(A\cap B)=0\ne P(A)P(B)$.
Non-example: a nonconstant random variable is not independent of itself, because $P(X\in S,\,X\in S)=P(X\in S)$ is not $P(X\in S)^2$ for some $S$.

reminder: A function between measurable spaces is measurable when the preimage of every measurable set is measurable.
definition: Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be sets with [sigma-algebras](c:sigma-algebra). A [function](c:function) $f:X\to Y$ is measurable when $f^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal{A}$ for every $B\in\mathcal{B}$. For real-valued $f$ with the Borel sigma-algebra on $\mathbb{R}$, it is enough to check the sets $\{f>a\}$ for $a\in\mathbb{R}$.
examples: Every continuous function between topological spaces is measurable for the Borel sigma-algebras.
The indicator function $1_A$ of a measurable set $A$ is measurable.
Pointwise limits of sequences of measurable real functions are measurable.
Non-example: the indicator of a Vitali set is not Lebesgue measurable, because the preimage of $\{1\}$ is a non-measurable set.

steps: Give two topological spaces their Borel sigma-algebras.
Let $f$ be continuous, so $f^{-1}(U)$ is open, hence Borel, for every open $U$.
The sets with a measurable preimage form a sigma-algebra that contains all open sets.
So every [continuous function](c:continuous-function) is measurable for the Borel sigma-algebras.
links.why: It shows that continuous functions are measurable functions for the Borel structure.

steps: Take a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal{F},P)$.
Take a measurable function $X:\Omega\to\mathbb{R}$.
Such an $X$ is a [random variable](c:random-variable), and $P$ gives it a distribution.
links.why: It shows that a random variable is a measurable function on a probability space.

steps: Take a measurable function $f$ on a measure space $(X,\mu)$.
Add the condition $\int|f|\,d\mu<\infty$.
Then $f$ is an [integrable function](c:integrable-function).
links.why: It shows that integrable functions are the measurable functions of finite absolute integral.

reminder: A graph is a set of vertices together with a set of edges, each edge joining two vertices.
definition: A simple graph is a pair $G=(V,E)$ of a [set](c:set) $V$ of vertices and a set $E$ of edges, where each edge is a two-element subset $\{u,v\}$ of $V$. Equivalently, $E$ is a symmetric irreflexive [relation](c:relation) on $V$; some authors also allow loops and repeated edges.
examples: The triangle graph has $V=\{1,2,3\}$ and all three pairs as edges.
The path on four vertices, the cycle $C_5$ and the complete graph $K_n$ are graphs.
Non-example: a set $V=\{1,2\}$ with the edge $\{1,3\}$ is not a graph, because every edge must join two vertices of $V$.

steps: Take a graph $G$.
Require a drawing of $G$ in the plane, with vertices as points and edges as curves.
Require that edges meet only at shared endpoints.
Then $G$ is a [planar graph](c:planar-graph).
links.why: It shows that planarity is a drawing condition on a graph.

steps: Take a graph $G$ with vertex set $V$.
Require a split $V=A\cup B$ into two disjoint parts.
Require that every edge has one end in $A$ and one end in $B$.
Then $G$ is a [bipartite graph](c:bipartite-graph).
links.why: It shows that bipartite graphs are the graphs whose vertices split into two sides with no edge inside a side.

reminder: An open set belongs to the topology; in a metric space it contains a ball around each of its points.
definition: In a [topological space](c:topological-space) $(X,\tau)$, a set is open when it belongs to the topology $\tau$. The topology contains $\emptyset$ and $X$, and it is closed under arbitrary unions and finite intersections. In a [metric space](c:metric-space), a set $U$ is open when for every $x\in U$ there is $r>0$ with the [ball](c:ball) $B(x,r)\subseteq U$.
examples: Open intervals $(a,b)$ in $\mathbb{R}$ and open balls in $\mathbb{R}^n$ are open.
In every space, $\emptyset$ and the whole space are open.
In the discrete topology, every subset is open.
Non-example: $[0,1)$ is not open in $\mathbb{R}$, because no ball around $0$ lies inside $[0,1)$.

steps: Let $U$ be an open set of a topological space.
The Borel [sigma-algebra](c:sigma-algebra) is the smallest sigma-algebra that contains all open sets.
So $U$ belongs to it, and $U$ is a [Borel set](c:borel-set).
links.why: It shows that every open set is measurable for the Borel structure.

steps: Take an open set $U$ of $X$.
Add the condition that the complement $X\setminus U$ is open too.
Then $U$ is both open and closed, a [clopen subset](c:clopen-subset).
links.why: It shows that a clopen set is an open set whose complement is also open.

reminder: A property holds almost everywhere when the points where it fails form a set of measure zero.
definition: Let $(X,\mathcal{A},\mu)$ be a [measure](c:measure) space. A property of the points of $X$ holds almost everywhere when the set of points where it fails lies inside a measurable set $N$ with $\mu(N)=0$.
examples: Two functions are equal almost everywhere when $\{f\ne g\}$ has measure zero; for example, the indicator of $\mathbb{Q}$ equals $0$ almost everywhere for Lebesgue measure, because $\mathbb{Q}$ is countable.
A monotone function on an interval is differentiable almost everywhere (Lebesgue).
Non-example: the property $x>0$ does not hold almost everywhere on $\mathbb{R}$ for Lebesgue measure, because the failing set $(-\infty,0]$ has infinite measure.

reminder: A scalar $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of a linear map $T$ when $Tv=\lambda v$ for some nonzero vector $v$.
definition: Let $T:V\to V$ be a [linear map](c:linear-map) on a [vector space](c:vector-space) $V$ over a field $F$. A scalar $\lambda\in F$ is an eigenvalue of $T$ when $Tv=\lambda v$ for some nonzero vector $v$, called an eigenvector. Equivalently, $T-\lambda I$ is not injective.
examples: The diagonal matrix $\mathrm{diag}(2,3)$ has eigenvalues $2$ and $3$, with eigenvectors $e_1$ and $e_2$.
A reflection of the plane across a line has eigenvalues $1$ and $-1$.
Non-example: a rotation of $\mathbb{R}^2$ by $90^\circ$ has no real eigenvalue, because it moves every nonzero vector off its own line; over $\mathbb{C}$ it has eigenvalues $\pm i$.
Non-example: $5$ is not an eigenvalue of $\mathrm{diag}(2,3)$, because $\mathrm{diag}(2,3)-5I$ is injective.

steps: Let $\lambda$ be an eigenvalue of $T$ with eigenvector $v\ne0$.
Then $(T-\lambda I)v=0$, so $T-\lambda I$ is not injective.
So $T-\lambda I$ has no inverse, and $\lambda$ lies in the [spectrum](c:spectrum-of-an-operator) of $T$.
On a finite-dimensional space, the spectrum consists of eigenvalues only.
links.why: It shows that an eigenvalue is a spectral value of the simplest kind, where $T-\lambda I$ fails to be injective.

reminder: A finite group is a [group](c:group) with finitely many elements.
definition: A finite group is a [group](c:group) $G$ whose underlying set is a [finite set](c:finite-set). The number of elements is the [order](c:order-of-a-group) $|G|$ of the group.
examples: The cyclic group $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ under addition is a finite group of order $n$.
The symmetric group $S_n$ is a finite group of order $n!$.
The rotations and reflections of a regular $n$-gon form a finite group of order $2n$.
Non-example: $(\mathbb{Z},+)$ is a group but not a finite group, because it has infinitely many elements.

steps: Start with a finite group $G$.
It has an associative operation, an identity and inverses, so it is a [group](c:group).
The extra condition is that $G$ has finitely many elements.
links.why: It shows that every result on groups applies to finite groups, which add counting tools such as Lagrange's theorem.

reminder: The derivative of a function at a point is the limit of its difference quotients there.
definition: For a [function](c:function) $f$ defined near $x$, the derivative is $f'(x)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}$ when this [limit](c:limit-of-a-function) exists. It is the slope of the tangent line to the graph of $f$ at $x$, and it gives the best linear approximation of $f$ near $x$.
examples: For $f(x)=x^2$ the difference quotient is $2x+h$, so $f'(x)=2x$.
$\exp'=\exp$ and $\sin'=\cos$.
Non-example: for $f(x)=|x|$ at $x=0$, the quotient is $1$ for $h>0$ and $-1$ for $h<0$, so $f'(0)$ does not exist.
Non-example: for $f(x)=x^{1/3}$ at $x=0$, the quotient $h^{-2/3}$ grows without bound, so there is no finite derivative.

steps: Take a function $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$, a point $x$ and a direction $v$.
The [directional derivative](c:directional-derivative) is $D_vf(x)=g'(0)$ for $g(t)=f(x+tv)$.
Choose $n=1$ and $v=1$.
Then $g(t)=f(x+t)$ and $D_vf(x)=f'(x)$, the ordinary derivative.
links.why: It shows that the one-variable derivative is the special case of the directional derivative in dimension one.

steps: Take $f(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ and fix every variable except $x_i$.
This gives a function $g(t)$ of one variable.
The [partial derivative](c:partial-derivative) $\partial f/\partial x_i$ is the derivative $g'$.
For $n=1$, nothing is fixed, so the partial derivative is the ordinary derivative.
links.why: It shows that partial derivatives reduce to the one-variable derivative.

reminder: An inner product space is a vector space with a positive definite inner product.
definition: An inner product space is a real or complex [vector space](c:vector-space) $V$ with an inner product $\langle u,v\rangle$: a symmetric [bilinear form](c:bilinear-form) over $\mathbb{R}$, or a [Hermitian form](c:hermitian-form) over $\mathbb{C}$, that is positive definite, so $\langle v,v\rangle>0$ for every $v\ne0$. The inner product gives the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ and the angle between vectors.
examples: $\mathbb{R}^n$ with the dot product $\langle x,y\rangle=\sum x_iy_i$ is an inner product space.
$\mathbb{C}^n$ with $\langle x,y\rangle=\sum x_i\bar y_i$ and $C([0,1])$ with $\int_0^1 f\bar g$ are inner product spaces.
Non-example: $\mathbb{R}^2$ with $\langle x,y\rangle=x_1y_1-x_2y_2$ is symmetric and bilinear but not positive definite, because $\langle(0,1),(0,1)\rangle=-1$.

steps: Take an inner product space $V$ with the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$.
Add the condition that every Cauchy sequence in $V$ converges in $V$.
Then $V$ is a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space).
links.why: It shows that a Hilbert space is a complete inner product space.

steps: Define the length $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ for every vector $v$.
Positive definiteness gives $\|v\|=0$ only for $v=0$.
The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality gives the triangle inequality, so $\|\cdot\|$ is a norm.
So $V$ is a [normed space](c:normed-space).
links.why: It shows that every inner product space is a normed space, with angles added.

steps: Take the vector space $\mathbb{R}^n$.
Give it the dot product $\langle x,y\rangle=\sum x_iy_i$.
This inner product is positive definite, so $\mathbb{R}^n$ with it is [Euclidean space](c:euclidean-space).
links.why: It shows that Euclidean space is the model inner product space.

reminder: A commutative ring is a [ring](c:ring) in which multiplication is commutative.
definition: A commutative ring is a [ring](c:ring) $R$ in which $ab=ba$ for all $a,b\in R$. So $R$ has an addition that makes it an abelian group and an associative multiplication that distributes over addition; most texts also require an identity $1$.
examples: The integers $\mathbb{Z}$ and the rings $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$ are commutative rings.
Every field is a commutative ring, and so is every polynomial ring $K[x]$.
The continuous real functions $C(X)$ with pointwise operations form a commutative ring.
Non-example: the ring of $2\times2$ real matrices is a ring but not commutative, because $E_{12}E_{21}\ne E_{21}E_{12}$.

steps: Start with a commutative ring $R$.
By definition, $R$ is a ring.
The extra condition is $ab=ba$ for all $a,b\in R$.
links.why: It shows that commutativity is the one condition added to the ring axioms.

steps: Take a commutative ring $R$ with $1\ne0$.
Add the condition that every nonzero element has a multiplicative inverse.
Then $R$ is a [field](c:field).
links.why: It shows that a field is a commutative ring in which division by nonzero elements works.

steps: Take a commutative ring $R$ with $1\ne0$.
Add the condition that $ab=0$ forces $a=0$ or $b=0$.
Then $R$ is an [integral domain](c:integral-domain).
links.why: It shows that an integral domain is a commutative ring with no zero divisors.

reminder: A Riemannian manifold is a [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold) whose tangent spaces carry smoothly varying inner products.
definition: A Riemannian manifold is a [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold) $M$ with a Riemannian metric $g$: an [inner product](c:inner-product-space) $g_p$ on each [tangent space](c:tangent-space) $T_pM$ that depends smoothly on the point $p$. The metric gives lengths of curves, angles between tangent vectors and a distance on each connected $M$.
examples: $\mathbb{R}^n$ with the Euclidean metric is a Riemannian manifold.
The sphere $S^n\subset\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ with the metric induced from $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ is a Riemannian manifold.
Every smooth submanifold of $\mathbb{R}^N$ with the induced metric is a Riemannian manifold.
Non-example: a manifold with a Lorentzian metric of signature $(-,+,+,+)$ is not Riemannian, because the form is not positive definite.

steps: Forget the metric $g$ of a Riemannian manifold $(M,g)$.
What remains is the manifold $M$ with its smooth atlas.
So $M$ is a smooth manifold, and the extra data is the metric $g$.
links.why: It shows that every Riemannian manifold is a smooth manifold with a metric added.

steps: Take a Riemannian manifold $(M,g)$.
Add an integrable complex structure $J$ with $g(Ju,Jv)=g(u,v)$.
Require that the 2-form $\omega(u,v)=g(Ju,v)$ is closed.
Then $M$ is a [Kähler manifold](c:kahler-manifold).
links.why: It shows that a Kähler manifold is a Riemannian manifold whose complex structure fits the metric and a closed 2-form.

reminder: The binomial coefficient $\binom{n}{k}$ counts the ways to choose $k$ elements from $n$ elements.
definition: For natural numbers $0\le k\le n$, the binomial coefficient $\binom{n}{k}$ is the number of $k$-element subsets of an $n$-element [finite set](c:finite-set). It equals $\frac{n!}{k!(n-k)!}$ with the [factorial](c:factorial), and it is the coefficient of $x^k$ in $(1+x)^n$.
examples: $\binom{5}{2}=10$, because there are $10$ pairs in a set of $5$ objects.
$\binom{n}{0}=\binom{n}{n}=1$ and $\binom{n}{1}=n$.
Pascal's rule holds: $\binom{n}{k}=\binom{n-1}{k-1}+\binom{n-1}{k}$.
Non-example: for $k>n$ the formula $n!/(k!(n-k)!)$ has no meaning, because $(n-k)!$ is undefined; the count of $k$-subsets is $0$ by convention.

steps: The [multinomial coefficient](c:multinomial-coefficient) $n!/(k_1!\cdots k_m!)$ counts splits of $n$ items into $m$ labeled groups of sizes $k_1,\dots,k_m$.
Take $m=2$, $k_1=k$ and $k_2=n-k$.
Choosing the first group fixes the second, so the count is the number of $k$-subsets.
So the multinomial coefficient equals $n!/(k!(n-k)!)=\binom{n}{k}$.
links.why: It shows that binomial coefficients are the two-group case of multinomial coefficients.

reminder: A set is closed when its complement is open.
definition: A subset $F$ of a [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ is closed when its complement $X\setminus F$ is an [open set](c:open-set). In a metric space, this means that the limit of every convergent sequence of points of $F$ lies in $F$.
examples: Closed intervals $[a,b]$ and single points are closed in $\mathbb{R}$.
The empty set and the whole space are both open and closed.
The zero set $\{x:f(x)=0\}$ of a continuous function $f$ is closed.
Non-example: $(0,1]$ is not closed in $\mathbb{R}$, because the sequence $1/n$ lies in it and has limit $0\notin(0,1]$.

steps: Let $F$ be a closed set, so its complement $U$ is open.
The Borel sigma-algebra contains $U$, because it contains all open sets.
A sigma-algebra is closed under complements, so it contains $F=X\setminus U$.
So $F$ is a [Borel set](c:borel-set).
links.why: It shows that every closed set is measurable for the Borel structure.

steps: Take a closed set $F$ of $X$.
Add the condition that $F$ is also open.
Then $F$ is a [clopen subset](c:clopen-subset).
links.why: It shows that a clopen set is a closed set that is also open.

reminder: A number field is a field extension of the rational numbers of finite degree.
definition: A number field is a [field](c:field) $K$ that contains the [rational numbers](c:rational-number) $\mathbb{Q}$ and has finite dimension $[K:\mathbb{Q}]$ as a vector space over $\mathbb{Q}$. That is, $K$ is a finite [field extension](c:field-extension) of $\mathbb{Q}$, and $[K:\mathbb{Q}]$ is its degree.
examples: $\mathbb{Q}$ itself is a number field of degree $1$.
$\mathbb{Q}(\sqrt2)=\{a+b\sqrt2:a,b\in\mathbb{Q}\}$ is a number field of degree $2$.
The cyclotomic fields $\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n)$ are number fields.
Non-example: $\mathbb{R}$ and $\mathbb{C}$ contain $\mathbb{Q}$ but have infinite degree over it, so they are not number fields.

steps: Let $K$ be a number field.
It contains $\mathbb{Q}$ as a subfield, so $K/\mathbb{Q}$ is a [field extension](c:field-extension).
The extra condition is that its degree $[K:\mathbb{Q}]$ is finite.
links.why: It shows that a number field is a finite extension of the base field $\mathbb{Q}$.

steps: Let $K=\mathbb{Q}(\zeta_n)$ be a [cyclotomic field](c:cyclotomic-field), where $\zeta_n$ is a primitive $n$-th root of unity.
The number $\zeta_n$ is a root of $x^n-1$, so it is algebraic of degree at most $n$.
So $K$ has finite degree over $\mathbb{Q}$.
Hence $K$ is a number field.
links.why: It shows that every cyclotomic field is a number field, so number field results apply to it.

reminder: A triangle is a [polygon](c:polygon) with three vertices, given by three non-collinear points joined by segments.
definition: A triangle is a [polygon](c:polygon) with three vertices: three points of a [plane](c:plane) that do not lie on one line, together with the three [line segments](c:line-segment) that join them. The segments are the sides, and in the Euclidean plane the angles at the vertices add up to $180^\circ$.
examples: The triangle with vertices $(0,0)$, $(1,0)$ and $(0,1)$ is a right triangle.
A triangle with sides $3$, $4$ and $5$ is a right triangle.
Non-example: the points $(0,0)$, $(1,1)$ and $(2,2)$ lie on one line, so they do not form a triangle.
Non-example: a square is a polygon with four vertices, so it is not a triangle.

steps: Start with a triangle $ABC$.
Its sides $AB$, $BC$ and $CA$ form a closed chain of segments that meet only at the vertices.
So $ABC$ is a polygon, with the extra condition that it has exactly three vertices.
links.why: It shows that a triangle is the polygon with the fewest vertices.

steps: Take a triangle $ABC$.
Add the condition $AB=BC=CA$.
Then $ABC$ is an [equilateral triangle](c:equilateral-triangle).
links.why: It shows that an equilateral triangle is a triangle with three equal sides.

steps: Take a triangle $ABC$.
Add the condition that all three angles are less than $90^\circ$.
Then $ABC$ is an [acute triangle](c:acute-triangle).
links.why: It shows that an acute triangle is a triangle with no right or obtuse angle.

reminder: A Lie algebra is a vector space with an alternating bilinear bracket that satisfies the Jacobi identity.
definition: A Lie algebra over a field $F$ is a [vector space](c:vector-space) $\mathfrak{g}$ with a [binary operation](c:binary-operation) $[x,y]$, the bracket, that is bilinear and alternating, so $[x,x]=0$. It also satisfies the Jacobi identity $[x,[y,z]]+[y,[z,x]]+[z,[x,y]]=0$.
examples: $\mathbb{R}^3$ with the cross product $[x,y]=x\times y$ is a Lie algebra.
The $n\times n$ matrices with $[A,B]=AB-BA$ form a Lie algebra.
The vector fields on a smooth manifold form a Lie algebra under the commutator of vector fields.
Non-example: the $n\times n$ matrices with the product $AB$ as bracket are not a Lie algebra, because $[A,A]=A^2$ is not zero in general.

steps: Take a Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$.
Add the condition that $[x,y]=0$ for all $x,y\in\mathfrak{g}$.
Then $\mathfrak{g}$ is an [abelian Lie algebra](c:abelian-lie-algebra), and the Jacobi identity holds at once.
links.why: It shows that an abelian Lie algebra is a Lie algebra with the zero bracket.

steps: Take a finite-dimensional Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$.
Add the condition that $\mathfrak{g}$ has no nonzero solvable ideal.
Then $\mathfrak{g}$ is a [semisimple Lie algebra](c:is-semisimple).
links.why: It shows that a semisimple Lie algebra is a Lie algebra with no solvable part.

reminder: A connected space cannot be written as the union of two disjoint nonempty open sets.
definition: A [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ is connected when it is not the union of two disjoint nonempty [open sets](c:open-set). Equivalently, the only subsets of $X$ that are both open and closed are $\emptyset$ and $X$.
examples: Every interval of $\mathbb{R}$ is connected, and so is $\mathbb{R}^n$.
The circle and the sphere are connected.
Non-example: $\mathbb{R}\setminus\{0\}$ is not connected, because $(-\infty,0)$ and $(0,\infty)$ are disjoint nonempty open sets with union the whole space.
Non-example: a discrete space with two points is not connected, because each point is an open set.

steps: Let $X$ be path connected, and suppose $X=U\cup V$ with $U$ and $V$ disjoint, nonempty and open.
Pick $a\in U$, $b\in V$ and a path $\gamma:[0,1]\to X$ from $a$ to $b$.
Then $[0,1]$ is the union of the disjoint nonempty open sets $\gamma^{-1}(U)$ and $\gamma^{-1}(V)$, which contradicts the connectedness of $[0,1]$.
So $X$ is connected.
links.why: It shows that every path connected space is connected, but not the other way round.

steps: Take a simply connected space $X$.
By definition, $X$ is path connected.
A path connected space is connected, so $X$ is connected.
links.why: It shows that simple connectivity adds a trivial fundamental group to connectedness.

reminder: First-order logic builds formulas from symbols, connectives and quantifiers that range over elements of a domain.
definition: First-order logic is a formal language whose formulas use symbols for [functions](c:function) and [relations](c:relation), equality, the connectives $\land,\lor,\lnot,\to$ and the quantifiers $\forall x$ and $\exists x$. A structure gives each symbol a meaning on a domain, and a formula is then true or false in the structure once its free variables have values.
examples: $\forall x\,\exists y\,(y>x)$ is a first-order sentence, and it is true in the structure $(\mathbb{N},<)$.
The axioms of groups and of fields are first-order sentences.
Non-example: the induction axiom that every subset of $\mathbb{N}$ containing $0$ and closed under successor equals $\mathbb{N}$ quantifies over subsets, so it is second-order, not first-order.

steps: Take a first-order formula; its quantifiers range over elements only.
Second-order logic also allows quantifiers over subsets or relations of the domain.
A formula without such quantifiers is also a second-order formula with the same meaning.
So first-order logic is the fragment of [second-order logic](c:second-order-logic) with no quantifiers over sets.
links.why: It shows that first-order logic is the restriction of second-order logic to quantifiers over elements.

reminder: A matrix is a rectangular array of entries from a ring that represents a linear map.
definition: An $m\times n$ matrix over a [ring](c:ring) $R$ is a rectangular array $A=(a_{ij})$ of entries $a_{ij}\in R$ with $m$ rows and $n$ columns. Over a field, and with chosen bases, $A$ represents the [linear map](c:linear-map) $x\mapsto Ax$ from $F^n$ to $F^m$.
examples: $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{pmatrix}$ is a $2\times2$ matrix over $\mathbb{Z}$.
The identity matrix $I_n$ represents the identity map.
A column vector with $n$ entries is an $n\times1$ matrix.
Non-example: an array with rows of different lengths is not a matrix, because every row must have the same number of entries.

steps: Take an $m\times n$ matrix $A$.
Add the condition $m=n$.
Then $A$ is a [square matrix](c:square-matrix), which maps a space to itself.
links.why: It shows that determinants, traces and eigenvalues apply to the square case of matrices.

reminder: A convex function lies below the chord between any two points of its graph.
definition: A function $f:C\to\mathbb{R}$ on a [convex set](c:convex-set) $C$ with values in the [real numbers](c:real-number) is convex when $f(tx+(1-t)y)\le tf(x)+(1-t)f(y)$ for all $x,y\in C$ and $t\in[0,1]$. Equivalently, the region above the graph of $f$ is a convex set.
examples: The functions $x^2$ and $e^x$ are convex on $\mathbb{R}$.
Every norm on a real vector space is a convex function.
The function $|x|$ is convex, although it is not differentiable at $0$.
Non-example: $x^3$ is not convex on $\mathbb{R}$, because for $x=-2$, $y=0$ and $t=1/2$ we get $f(-1)=-1>-4=(f(-2)+f(0))/2$.

steps: Take a convex function $f$ on a convex set $C$.
Add the condition that the inequality is strict whenever $x\ne y$ and $0<t<1$.
Then $f$ is a [strictly convex function](c:strictly-convex-function).
links.why: It shows that strict convexity rules out flat pieces in the graph.

reminder: A subset is dense when its [closure](c:closure) is the whole space.
definition: A subset $D$ of a [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ is dense when its [closure](c:closure) is $X$. Equivalently, every nonempty [open set](c:open-set) of $X$ contains a point of $D$; in a metric space, every point of $X$ is a limit of points of $D$.
examples: $\mathbb{Q}$ is dense in $\mathbb{R}$.
The polynomials are dense in $C([0,1])$ for the sup norm (Weierstrass).
Every space is dense in itself.
Non-example: $\mathbb{Z}$ is not dense in $\mathbb{R}$, because the open interval $(0.2,0.8)$ contains no integer.

reminder: The determinant of a square matrix is nonzero exactly when the matrix is invertible.
definition: The determinant is the unique function from the $n\times n$ [matrices](c:matrix) over a field to the field that is multilinear and alternating in the columns and sends the identity to $1$. It equals $\sum_{\sigma\in S_n}\operatorname{sgn}(\sigma)\prod_i a_{i\sigma(i)}$, and $\det A\ne0$ exactly when the [square matrix](c:square-matrix) $A$ is invertible.
examples: For a $2\times2$ matrix, $\det\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}=ad-bc$.
The determinant of a triangular matrix is the product of its diagonal entries.
The number $|\det A|$ is the factor by which $A$ scales volumes.
Non-example: the determinant is not additive; for $A=B=I_2$ we get $\det(A+B)=4$ but $\det A+\det B=2$.

reminder: A martingale is an adapted process whose expected next value, given the past, equals the present value.
definition: A martingale is a [stochastic process](c:stochastic-process) $(X_n)$ of integrable [random variables](c:random-variable) that is adapted to a [filtration](c:filtration) $(\mathcal{F}_n)$ and satisfies $E[X_{n+1}\mid\mathcal{F}_n]=X_n$. This identity uses the [conditional expectation](c:conditional-expectation): given the past, the process has no drift.
examples: The fortune in a fair game, $X_n=\xi_1+\dots+\xi_n$ with independent steps of mean zero, is a martingale.
For an integrable random variable $Z$, the process $E[Z\mid\mathcal{F}_n]$ is a martingale (a Doob martingale).
Non-example: a random walk with steps of mean $p>0$ is not a martingale, because $E[X_{n+1}\mid\mathcal{F}_n]=X_n+p\ne X_n$.

reminder: A power series is a series $\sum_{n\ge0}a_n(x-c)^n$ whose terms are powers of $x-c$ times coefficients.
definition: A power series centered at $c$ is a [series](c:series) $\sum_{n\ge0}a_n(x-c)^n$ with coefficients $a_n$ in a field such as $\mathbb{R}$ or $\mathbb{C}$. It is a [polynomial](c:polynomial) that may have infinitely many terms. It defines a function where it converges, or it is a formal object that needs no convergence.
examples: $\sum_{n\ge0}x^n$ is a power series, and it converges to $1/(1-x)$ for $|x|<1$.
$e^x=\sum_{n\ge0}x^n/n!$ is a power series that converges for every $x$.
The formal power series ring $K[[x]]$ holds power series with no convergence condition.
Non-example: $\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}a_nx^n$ with infinitely many negative powers is a Laurent series, not a power series.

steps: Take the power series $\sum a_n(x-c)^n$ and fix a number $x$.
The terms $a_n(x-c)^n$ form a sequence of numbers.
Their sum is a [series](c:series) in the sense of partial sums.
links.why: It shows that a power series gives a series of numbers at each value of $x$.

steps: Start with a power series $\sum_{n\ge0}a_n(x-c)^n$.
Put $a_n=0$ for every negative $n$.
This is a [Laurent series](c:laurent-series) with no negative powers.
links.why: It shows that a power series is a Laurent series without negative powers.

steps: Take a function $f$ with derivatives of all orders at $c$.
Set the coefficients to $a_n=f^{(n)}(c)/n!$ for each $n$.
Then $\sum a_n(x-c)^n$ is a power series, the [Taylor series](c:taylor-series) of $f$ at $c$.
links.why: It shows that a Taylor series is a power series with coefficients from derivatives.

reminder: A self-adjoint operator is an operator on a Hilbert space that equals its own adjoint.
definition: A linear operator $A$ with dense domain $D(A)$ on a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) $H$ is self-adjoint when $A=A^*$, where $A^*$ is its [adjoint](c:adjoint-operator), and the domains of $A$ and $A^*$ are equal. For a bounded operator on all of $H$, this means $\langle Ax,y\rangle=\langle x,Ay\rangle$ for all $x,y\in H$.
examples: A real symmetric matrix and a complex Hermitian matrix are self-adjoint operators on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and $\mathbb{C}^n$.
Multiplication by a bounded real measurable function on $L^2$ is self-adjoint.
Non-example: the rotation $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix}$ on $\mathbb{R}^2$ has $A^*=-A\ne A$, so it is not self-adjoint.
Non-example: $-i\,d/dx$ on smooth functions on $[0,1]$ that vanish at both ends is symmetric but not self-adjoint, because its adjoint has a larger domain.

steps: Take a self-adjoint operator $A$ on $H$.
Add the condition $\langle Ax,x\rangle\ge0$ for every $x$ in the domain.
Then $A$ is a [positive operator](c:positive-operator).
links.why: It shows that a positive operator is a self-adjoint operator with nonnegative quadratic form.

steps: Let $A$ be self-adjoint, so $A=A^*$.
Then $\langle Ax,y\rangle=\langle x,Ay\rangle$ for all $x,y$ in the domain of $A$.
So $A$ is a [symmetric operator](c:symmetric-operator).
Self-adjointness adds that the domain of $A^*$ is no larger than the domain of $A$.
links.why: It shows that self-adjoint operators are the symmetric operators with no domain gap.

steps: Let $A$ be a bounded self-adjoint operator, so $A^*=A$.
Then we get $AA^*=A^2=A^*A$ by substitution.
So $A$ commutes with its adjoint, and $A$ is a [normal operator](c:normal-operator).
links.why: It shows that self-adjoint operators inherit the spectral theory of normal operators.

reminder: The convex hull of a set is the smallest convex set that contains it.
definition: The convex hull of a subset $S$ of a real [vector space](c:vector-space) is the smallest [convex set](c:convex-set) that contains $S$, which is the intersection of all convex sets that contain $S$. Equivalently, it is the set of all convex combinations $t_1x_1+\dots+t_kx_k$ with $x_i\in S$, $t_i\ge0$ and $\sum t_i=1$.
examples: The convex hull of two points is the line segment between them.
The convex hull of three points of the plane that are not on one line is the filled triangle.
The convex hull of the unit circle is the closed unit disk.
Non-example: the circle is not its own convex hull, because it is not convex; its hull is the disk.

steps: For a subset $S$ of a vector space $V$, let $\mathrm{conv}(S)$ be its convex hull.
Then $S\subseteq\mathrm{conv}(S)$, and $S\subseteq T$ gives $\mathrm{conv}(S)\subseteq\mathrm{conv}(T)$.
Also $\mathrm{conv}(\mathrm{conv}(S))=\mathrm{conv}(S)$, because the hull is already convex.
So $\mathrm{conv}$ is a [closure operator](c:closure-operator) on the subsets of $V$.
links.why: It shows that the convex hull is a closure operator, so general facts about closures apply to it.

reminder: A fixed point of a map $f$ is a point $x$ with $f(x)=x$.
definition: Let $f:X\to X$ be a [function](c:function) from a set to itself. A fixed point of $f$ is an element $x\in X$ with $f(x)=x$. For a real function, these are the points where the graph meets the line $y=x$.
examples: $f(x)=x^2$ on $\mathbb{R}$ has the two fixed points $0$ and $1$.
The identity map fixes every point.
A rotation of the plane about the origin by a nonzero angle has exactly one fixed point, the origin.
Non-example: $f(x)=x+1$ on $\mathbb{R}$ has no fixed point, because $x+1=x$ is impossible.

steps: A point $x$ is periodic of period $n$ when $f^n(x)=x$.
Take $n=1$; then $f^1(x)=x$ is the fixed point condition.
So a fixed point is a [periodic point](c:periodic-point) of period $1$.
links.why: It shows that fixed points are the periodic points of period one.

reminder: A planar graph has a drawing in the plane in which edges meet only at shared endpoints.
definition: A [graph](c:graph) is planar when it can be drawn in the [plane](c:plane) with vertices as distinct points and edges as curves between their end vertices, so that edges meet only at shared endpoints. By Kuratowski's theorem, this holds exactly when the graph has no subgraph that is a subdivision of $K_5$ or $K_{3,3}$.
examples: Every tree and every cycle is planar.
The complete graph $K_4$ is planar: draw one vertex inside the triangle of the other three.
The graph of the cube is planar.
Non-example: $K_5$ is not planar, because a planar simple graph with $v\ge3$ vertices has at most $3v-6$ edges, and $K_5$ has $10>9$ edges.

steps: Start with a planar graph $G$.
It has vertices and edges, so it is a [graph](c:graph).
The extra condition is a drawing in the plane in which edges meet only at shared endpoints.
links.why: It shows that planarity is a drawing condition added to a graph.

reminder: A series is the formal sum of the terms of a sequence, and its value is the limit of its partial sums.
definition: The series $\sum_{n\ge0}a_n$ of a [sequence](c:sequence) $(a_n)$ of numbers has the partial sums $s_N=a_0+\dots+a_N$. It converges to $s$ when the [limit of the sequence](c:limit-of-a-sequence) $(s_N)$ is $s$, and then $s$ is its value.
examples: The geometric series $\sum x^n$ converges to $1/(1-x)$ for $|x|<1$.
The series $\sum 1/n^2$ converges, and its value is $\pi^2/6$.
Non-example: the harmonic series $\sum 1/n$ does not converge, because its partial sums grow without bound.
Non-example: $\sum(-1)^n$ does not converge, because its partial sums alternate between $1$ and $0$.

steps: Take a power series $\sum a_n(x-c)^n$ and fix a number $x$.
The terms $a_n(x-c)^n$ form a sequence of numbers.
Their sum is a [series](c:series) with partial sums, so each value of $x$ gives a series.
links.why: It shows that a power series is a family of series, one for each value of $x$.

steps: Let $\sum ar^n$ be a geometric series, so $a_n=ar^n$.
Its terms form a sequence, so it is a series.
Its partial sums are $a(1-r^{N+1})/(1-r)$ for $r\ne1$, and they converge exactly when $|r|<1$ if $a\ne0$.
links.why: It shows that the geometric series is the series whose convergence we can decide in closed form.

reminder: A circle is the set of points in a plane at a fixed distance from a fixed point.
definition: A circle with centre $c$ and radius $r>0$ is the set of points of the Euclidean plane at [distance](c:distance) $r$ from $c$. In [Euclidean space](c:euclidean-space) $\mathbb{R}^2$ with $c=(a,b)$, it is the set where $(x-a)^2+(y-b)^2=r^2$.
examples: The unit circle is the set where $x^2+y^2=1$.
The circle with centre $(1,2)$ and radius $3$ has the equation $(x-1)^2+(y-2)^2=9$.
Non-example: the disk $x^2+y^2\le1$ is not a circle, because it contains points at distance less than $1$ from the centre.
Non-example: the set $x^2+y^2=0$ is one point, not a circle, because the radius must be positive.

steps: Cut a cone by a plane that is perpendicular to its axis.
The section is the set where $(x-a)^2+(y-b)^2=r^2$ in suitable coordinates.
This is a polynomial equation of degree $2$ in $x$ and $y$.
So a circle is a [conic section](c:conic-section), the case with eccentricity $0$.
links.why: It shows that a circle is the conic section of eccentricity zero.

steps: The $n$-sphere is the set of points at distance $r$ from a centre in $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$.
Take the case $n=1$.
Then the set lies in $\mathbb{R}^2$ and is a circle.
So a circle is the [sphere](c:sphere) of dimension $1$.
links.why: It shows that a circle is the one-dimensional sphere.

reminder: A metric space is complete when every Cauchy sequence converges to a point of the space.
definition: A [metric space](c:metric-space) $(X,d)$ is complete when every [Cauchy sequence](c:cauchy-sequence) in $X$ has a limit in $X$. That is, if $d(x_m,x_n)\to0$ as $m,n\to\infty$, then there is $x\in X$ with $d(x_n,x)\to0$.
examples: $\mathbb{R}$ and $\mathbb{R}^n$ with the usual metric are complete.
Every compact metric space is complete.
The space $C([0,1])$ with the sup metric is complete.
Non-example: $\mathbb{Q}$ with the usual metric is not complete, because decimal approximations of $\sqrt2$ form a Cauchy sequence with no limit in $\mathbb{Q}$.

steps: Start with a complete metric space $(X,d)$.
By definition, it is a [metric space](c:metric-space).
The extra condition is that every Cauchy sequence in $X$ converges in $X$.
links.why: It shows that completeness is the one condition added to a metric space.

steps: Take a Banach space $X$ with its norm.
Define $d(x,y)=\|x-y\|$, which is a metric on $X$.
By definition, every Cauchy sequence for $d$ converges in $X$.
So $(X,d)$ is a complete metric space.
links.why: It shows that every Banach space is a complete metric space, so the Baire theorem applies to it.

reminder: An ideal is an additive subgroup of a ring that absorbs multiplication by every element of the ring.
definition: An ideal of a [ring](c:ring) $R$ is an additive [subgroup](c:subgroup) $I$ of $R$ such that $ra\in I$ and $ar\in I$ for all $r\in R$ and $a\in I$. Ideals are the subsets that one can divide out: $R/I$ is again a ring.
examples: $n\mathbb{Z}$ is an ideal of $\mathbb{Z}$ for each integer $n$.
In $K[x]$, the multiples of a fixed polynomial form an ideal.
The kernel of every ring homomorphism is an ideal.
Non-example: $\mathbb{Z}$ is a subring of $\mathbb{Q}$ but not an ideal, because $\tfrac12\cdot1\notin\mathbb{Z}$.

steps: Take an ideal $P$ of a commutative ring $R$.
Add the condition $P\ne R$.
Add the condition that $ab\in P$ implies $a\in P$ or $b\in P$.
Then $P$ is a [prime ideal](c:prime-ideal).
links.why: It shows that a prime ideal is a proper ideal that behaves like a prime number.

steps: Take an ideal $I$ of a commutative ring $R$.
Add the condition that $I=aR$ for one element $a$.
Then $I$ is a [principal ideal](c:principal-ideal), generated by $a$.
links.why: It shows that a principal ideal is an ideal with a single generator.

steps: Let $R$ be commutative and view $R$ as a module over itself.
An ideal $I$ is closed under addition and under multiplication by every $r\in R$.
These are exactly the conditions for a [submodule](c:submodule) of $R$.
So the ideals of $R$ are the submodules of $R$ as a module over itself.
links.why: It shows that an ideal is a submodule of the ring itself, so module results apply to ideals.

reminder: An open cover of a space is a family of open sets whose union is the whole space.
definition: An open cover of a [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ is a [family](c:family-of-sets) $\{U_i\}_{i\in I}$ of [open sets](c:open-set) of $X$ with $\bigcup_iU_i=X$. A subcover is a subfamily whose union is still $X$.
examples: The family $\{(n-1,n+1):n\in\mathbb{Z}\}$ is an open cover of $\mathbb{R}$.
For every space $X$, the one-member family $\{X\}$ is an open cover.
The open balls $B(x,1)$ for $x\in X$ form an open cover of a metric space $X$.
Non-example: $\{(0,1),(1,2)\}$ is not an open cover of $(0,2)$, because the point $1$ lies in no member.

reminder: A subgroup is a subset of a group that contains the identity and is closed under products and inverses.
definition: A [subset](c:subset) $H$ of a [group](c:group) $G$ is a subgroup when $e\in H$, when $ab\in H$ for all $a,b\in H$, and when $a^{-1}\in H$ for all $a\in H$. Then $H$ is itself a group under the operation of $G$.
examples: The multiples $n\mathbb{Z}$ form a subgroup of $(\mathbb{Z},+)$.
The even permutations form a subgroup $A_n$ of the symmetric group $S_n$.
Every group has the trivial subgroup $\{e\}$ and the whole group as subgroups.
Non-example: $\mathbb{N}$ is a subset of $(\mathbb{Z},+)$ that is closed under addition, but it is not a subgroup, because $-1$ is missing.

steps: Take a subgroup $H$ of a group $G$.
Add the condition $gHg^{-1}=H$ for every $g\in G$.
Then $H$ is a [normal subgroup](c:normal-subgroup), and its cosets form a quotient group.
links.why: It shows that a normal subgroup is a subgroup that conjugation preserves.

steps: Take a finite group $G$ of order $p^km$ with $p\nmid m$.
Choose a subgroup $H$ of $G$ of order $p^k$.
Then $H$ is a [Sylow subgroup](c:sylow-subgroup), with the largest possible $p$-power order.
links.why: It shows that a Sylow subgroup is a subgroup of the largest prime power order.

reminder: Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function that picks one element from each set.
definition: The axiom of choice says that for every [family of sets](c:family-of-sets) $(A_i)_{i\in I}$ with each $A_i$ nonempty, there is a [function](c:function) $f$ on $I$ with $f(i)\in A_i$ for all $i$. Equivalently, the [Cartesian product](c:cartesian-product) $\prod_iA_i$ is nonempty.
examples: For a finite family of nonempty sets, a choice function exists without the axiom, because one can pick the elements one at a time.
For nonempty subsets of $\mathbb{N}$, the rule take the least element is a choice function, so no axiom is needed.
Zorn's lemma and the well-ordering theorem are equivalent to the axiom of choice.
Non-example: for the family of all nonempty subsets of $\mathbb{R}$, the rule take the least element is not a choice function, because $(0,1)$ has no least element.

steps: Let $(A_n)_{n\in\mathbb{N}}$ be a countable family of nonempty sets.
This is a family indexed by the set $I=\mathbb{N}$.
The axiom of choice gives a choice function $f$ with $f(n)\in A_n$ for all $n$.
So [countable choice](c:countable-choice) follows.
links.why: It shows that countable choice is the case of the axiom of choice for countable families.

steps: Let $(A_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family of nonempty sets with $I$ finite.
The axiom of choice gives a choice function $f$ with $f(i)\in A_i$.
So [finite choice](c:finite-choice) follows.
links.why: It shows that finite choice is the case of the axiom of choice for finite families.
